words: Picture yourself 40,000
years in the past.
The mammoths didn't get you today. The cold
didn't either. Now the sun
slips behind the hills, the
fire crackles, and the night stretches
out ahead of you. Six long hours
with no phone, no feed,
no screen of any kind.
Nothing to do at all.
And strangely, that nothing is
exactly what's going to make
you invent fun. Music,
gambling, board games,
even the first movie night. All of it
starts right here, with a bored
human sitting in the dark.
Here's the thing most of us get
wrong about our ancestors. We tend to
imagine life back then as
one endless emergency. Saber-toothed cats
behind every rock. Frostbite.
Hunger. A fight for survival
from sunrise to sunset.
Hollywood loves that version. The
evidence doesn't. When anthropologists sat
down with modern hunter-gatherer groups
and actually tallied up the hours,
the results were surprising.
Hunting, foraging, hauling water,
sharpening tools. All the essential
work added up to somewhere around
four to six hours a day.
After that, the job was basically finished.
The afternoon was free.
That's a shorter workday than most of
us have today. Which leaves
you with a strange problem.
Your brain is an expensive organ.
It eats up roughly a fifth of
your body's energy. And it hates sitting idle.
It's built to search for patterns and
crave something new. Give it hours
of daylight and a long
dark evening with nothing in them,
and it starts to protest. Staring at the
ground isn't going to cut it.
That restless feeling has a name.
Boredom. And far from
being a modern problem, boredom may be
one of the oldest forces pushing
our species forward. Its first
big invention? Music.
In a cave in southern
Germany's Swabian Jura, researchers uncovered
something remarkable. A flute
carved from mammoth tusk
around 40,000 years old.
Mammoth ivory is tough,
dense material. A nightmare to
work even with today's metal tools.
Yet someone armed only with sharpened
stone split the tusk in two,
scraped out the inside,
joined the halves back together, and bored a
row of carefully placed finger holes.
That could easily have taken
dozens or even hundreds of hours.
One tiny slip and all that
work would crack. And for what?
A flute won't bring down a cave bear.
It won't keep the rain off.
Its only purpose was to make
a sound that felt good to hear
in the dark. Consider how
wild that is. Back then, a small
cut could turn deadly. And still, someone
spent all that time and effort
on something that existed purely
for the mood. Music did more
than fill the silence, though.
It held groups together.
Play a beat around the fire with other people,
and your breathing starts to match theirs.
Your bodies move together. Even your brain
activity begins to line up.
A scattered band of nervous,
vulnerable apes becomes a team.
On the longest winter nights,
that shared rhythm may have been what
kept people from turning on each other.
Still, even the best song gets repetitive.
And we're a species built
for thrills. Our bodies are
designed to handle the rush of chasing
down dangerous animals. So picture it.
You're warm. You're fed.
You're safe. And you haven't felt
that rush in days. You're restless.
You're itching for something to happen.
What fills the gap?
A game. Archaeologists keep turning
up one particular kind of object
at sites all over the world,
separated by vast distances and
thousands of years. Small ankle bones
from sheep, goats, and deer.
These are astragali, better
known as knuckle bones.
Their uneven shape means they settle on a different side
depending on how they're tossed.
In other words, they're random.
They're dice made by nature.
And as soon as people noticed that,
the betting began. Roll higher than
me and you win my arrows.
Or my fur. Or my piece
of tonight's dinner. Now imagine losing
your warm fur on a bad throw,
with winter on the way. Thousands of
years before coins, casinos, or
stock exchanges, people were staking
the very things that kept them alive
on the tumble of a little bone.
Greed wasn't really the point.
The thrill was. Risk made
a quiet evening feel exciting.
Games kept evolving from there.
Roughly 5,000 years ago
in Egypt, one of the most
popular pastimes was Senet, played on a
board of 30 squares, with throwing sticks
deciding how far your pieces moved.
At first, it was just a race to the finish.
But over many centuries, the
game took on a deeper meaning.
The board came to represent the underworld,
and certain squares became dangers
the soul had to get past.
Moving your pieces became a kind of practice run
for the journey after death.
It mattered so much that Senet
boards were buried with the dead,
including several in the tomb of Tutankhamen.
A simple pastime had become
something sacred. Not everyone wants
to play, of course. Sometimes you just
want to sit back and watch something.
And while there were no movie theaters
in the Stone Age, there was something
not far off. Deep inside
Chauvet Cave in southern France,
far from any daylight,
the walls are covered with lions,
rhinos, and horses painted more than
30,000 years ago. Under modern
electric lights, they look like
a still gallery. But they were never meant
to be seen that way. Their creators
saw them by flickering firelight.
Move a flame across them, and
the animals seem to come alive.
Extra legs drawn on top of
each other suddenly look like galloping.
Shadows shift and stretch.
Imagine sitting there in the dark,
listening to a story about a hunt,
while the walls appear to move around you.
That's about as close to the first
cinema as it gets. For most of
human history, then, entertainment
cost nothing. Music, games,
and stories were homemade
and shared. That changed
with one invention. The city.
Roughly 6,000 years ago
in Mesopotamia, people began leaving small
groups of a few dozen and settling
into towns of thousands in
places like Uruk. In a band
of 40, everyone is family or
close to it. You'd never ask a
relative to pay you for a song.
But a city is full of strangers.
And dealing with strangers means trading.
Fairly quickly, fun turned
into business. Music now came
from paid performers at the tavern.
Beer had a price,
settled in barley or silver.
So did sex. Mesopotamian records
mention taverns, drinking debts,
and paid sex work alongside
everyday entries like grain prices
and workers' wages. Our oldest cravings
had become things you could
buy and sell. What once got
people through long Ice Age nights
grew into entire industries.
Bone flutes led to music streaming.
Knuckle bones led to Las Vegas.
Fire-lit cave walls led to
Netflix picking your next show.
The fire is gone.
The craving never left. Because the brain
doing the craving is the
same one our ancestors had.
Inside your head is essentially the same machine
that drove someone to carve a flute
from a mammoth tusk. So when you
find yourself scrolling late at night,
chasing one more laugh or one more
hit of dopamine, go easy on yourself.
Nothing is wrong with you.
You're simply doing what people have always
done when the sun goes down.
You're fighting off the dark.
